The problem with this film will always be that Yojimbo is obviously better (and somehow, despite being longer, a great deal more urgently-paced), but despite its extraordinarily close resemblance to its model, this is happily much less redundant than one could easily fear. For one thing, Clint Eastwood's vibe is completely different than Mifune Toshirō's, not in a way that I'm prepared to call either one "better", but it does mean that there's a sneering nihilistic bitterness to Leone's vision of pointless cycles of violence that Kurosawa's more sardonic but also more human vision doesn't quite aim for. For another thing, color really changes this: Leone didn't invent the Italian-production-shot-in-Spain Western, but he pushed it to astonishing new heights, the hot yellow of the dead earth creating a feeling of dusty exhaustion beneath the taunting coolness of the blue sky that makes the films feel set in a mythic neverwhen of endless desert studded with barely-extant towns (which is, for that matter, another very consequential difference: Kurosawa's film takes place in a historicized Japan, but Leone's takes place in a hazy, hellish fantasy of The American Wild West, and it just feels dreamier). This was my first chance to watch the entirety of the Arrow restoration from 2025, and it's a real "scales fall from my eyes" moment - just jaw-dropping how overwhelming the earth tones are when they've been calibrated and shaded properly. Would absolutely be a classic even if Leone hadn't ever stepped foot on a film set again, but in context, one can't help but note that this is a very exploratory first effort: the aggressive close-ups slashed together in brutal jab-jab-jab edits are a remarkable gesture (and one that isn't in any way indebted to Yojimbo ), but you can tell he hasn't figured out how to balance them yet, either as compositions or within the edit; they're very assertive but they don't have the weight that they'll have in the two follow-ups. Still, I think is to be celebrated for creating a template that could be built upon to such magnificent effect rather than condemned for not immediately representing the high-water-mark of its genre. Also, Ennio Morricone's work here is totally awe-inspiring , lonely windy whistling, raspy male vocalizations, and menacing Mexican & Texan instrumentation combining to create a sonic concept for "The West" that as far as I know was invented in this movie and has, to me at least, absolutely defined the way I think about how that time and place sound. And amazingly, this is another respect in which both sequels clearly improve on it! ( Previously reviewed at Alternate Ending )

Let’s just say the first freaking second already started with a bang - a wonderful soundtrack by the great Ennio Morricone! The plot is straight to the point and our antihero is a great man. The supporting cast is so-so, besides Silvanito and Piripero. The scenery of Spain in the background is breathtaking and set design is TOP! I love that it is 1h and 30min long, the perfect length. That was an extremely good film. I bought the entire trilogy right away and this definitely made me excited for more. I wouldn't call myself a huge Western fan because I haven't actually seen that many, but I just love the concept of Westerns. Cowboys, revolvers, outlaws, horses, robberies, all that stuff just gets me. And A Fistful of Dollars absolutely delivered on everything I like about the genre. First of all, Clint Eastwood is just so cool. The poncho, the horse, the cold and almost stoic stare, while still having this really dry sense of humor. I loved every time he pushed the poncho aside and you could see the revolver and his hand ready to draw. It only happens a couple of times, but it looks so cool. San Miguel also looks amazing. As far as I know, it was shot in Spain, but the whole place just looks perfect. And yes, this is probably the most basic call imaginable, but watching this immediately made me want to play Red Dead Redemption 2. If there was a 60 FPS upgrade on PS5, I would probably be playing it right now. The story is pretty compact. You basically have this outlaw arriving in a town where two gangs are fighting each other, and he immediately starts looking for ways to make money off both of them. He gets to know both sides, befriends the bartender, plays the gangs against each other and just keeps collecting money. The whole thing with the two corpses was great. I especially liked the Rojos. Ramón was so cool. That actor was incredible. Honestly, everyone in this movie just looks like they belong there. Every face, every outfit, every character. They all look like they actually came from this place. I love the cowboy pants, the boots, the ponchos, the revolvers, the belts. Everything just looks right. Even the stagecoach robbery with the Gatling gun was awesome, although the aim was maybe a little questionable. But my absolute favorite thing about the movie is the close-ups. Bro, these faces. Everyone just stares into the camera with these incredibly tough, cold expressions while the music keeps building and you just sit there waiting for someone to draw their revolver. You can feel the tension building until someone finally shoots. These close-ups are probably my favorite shots in the entire movie. The faces just fit this world so perfectly. And the ending is so good. The buildings explode, smoke fills the street and Clint Eastwood just walks out of it. Ramón shoots him and he keeps getting back up because he has that metal plate underneath his poncho. Then he throws Ramón's own line back at him and they have this final rifle versus revolver duel. It's simple, but it looks so damn cool. I also loved the humor. Near the end, when Eastwood walks into that building, shoots everyone and then this cat just runs away, I don't even know why, but that absolutely got me. And obviously, Morricone. Bro, what did you do? That whistling is permanently stuck in my head now. Once you've heard it, there is no going back. The soundtrack sounds absolutely incredible and fits the movie perfectly. Something I thought about a lot while watching this is how I usually approach movies. I tend to look for sociological, political or philosophical ideas and try to understand what a film is doing on some kind of meta level. And I don't think A Fistful of Dollars has this huge deeper layer, at least not from the sociological perspective I usually look for. You can probably find smaller things, but overall it felt pretty thin in that regard. But this movie also reinforced something for me. A film doesn't necessarily need that kind of depth to be great. Sometimes a movie can just be incredibly good at being a movie. And maybe I should focus even more on analyzing films on that cinematic level when that's the level they're actually offering me. Because that's where A Fistful of Dollars completely got me. The only thing really keeping it from a 5 for me is that I would've liked a little more in terms of what it actually has to say. Other than that, I genuinely don't have much to complain about. I watched the 4K restoration too, and it looked amazing. I can't wait for For a Few Dollars More and The Good, the Bad and the Ugly. This is just really good cinema.

Reel Review: A Fistful of Dollars is a stellar remake. It is a rock ‘n’ roll western about an anti-hero out to make money by pitting two rival gang against each other. Leone expertly crafts a tense film with a cynical and deadly attitude. It’s the perfect flick for the transformative 1960s era which builds on the myth of the American western from the perspective of Italian and Spanish filmmakers. Few films have had such impact from its iconic score to the stoic lead character. The movie’s working title was “The Magnificent Stranger” and Eastwood effortlessly plays that wandering loner. He’s cool, clever, confident, charismatic, and cold blooded. The role shot him to superstardom and I can’t imagine anyone else playing him. The entire cast is made up of some solid actors from all over the map. The script is extremely similar to Yojimbo, yet with a setting and style all its own. The extreme closeups are one of the aspects that make this movie stand out along with the brutal action scenes. Morricone’s score is also an element that is absolutely recognizable. The movie brings a gritty and dirty look to the old west due to excellent sets, locations, costumes, hair, and makeup. Boredom never sets in thanks to good editing, bursts of violence, and a perfect mix of humor and tension. This is a groundbreaking movie and it remains an enjoyable watch. The Man With No Name trilogy Blu-ray set is good. There are a few issues with the video and audio, but it is a solid presentation overall. A few bonus features are included. The best element is the commentary which bring out so much detail into the story of the making of the film as well as the film itself and it’s historical impact. It may be worth finding a 4K edition, but make sure it includes this commentary. Had already seen The Good The Bad and the Ugly, and enjoyed it so much that I bought the Arrow 4K set. Assuming the other two films look like this one, it’s safe to say that their restorations are incredible. Obviously Fistful isn’t anywhere near as epic as the last film in the trilogy (it’s only half as long, for starters), but it’s just as fun, and just as occasionally silly, and just as grounded in its violence, despite that silliness. Why can’t we go back to the days where our heroes get their asses kicked because they are, in fact, egregiously outnumbered, and aren’t in fact, quite as clever as they think they are. Maybe, beyond being tall, silent, and handsome, that’s part of Clint’s appeal here? Even if it looks “cool” or “badass”, it just isn’t all that narratively compelling to watch a so-called hero never take any damage from their beating. We get what, 5-10 minutes of Clint having to crawl across town because he’s been so thoroughly whipped? When’s the last time that happened in a major film? The horse “chase” sequence after The Man With No Name  (TMWNN) secrets the family away is wonderful, not just for the sight and sound of it, but for the fact that there isn’t some obligatory bit of dialogue where Clint is forced to tell the family that he has to make it back before the evil crew so he can get away with his clever plan. Even better, we don’t get some sort of crowing monologue from the villain when he’s caught anyway. Hooray visual storytelling, may you return one day. Someone much smarter than me already pointed out the inherent silliness/impossible coolness of TMWNN repeatedly saying “Aim for the heart” in the final showdown, but for me it’s the fact that he just spins the revolver after loading it, only for it to perfectly land on the right chamber that really completes the fantasy.
